title: ADR-000: Common evaluation criteria for all tool selections
description:
Define the shared evaluation template that every ADR (001–010) will apply. Produces a reusable criteria rubric and a short prose section that each ADR includes by reference.

## Why this exists

Each ADR will evaluate different tools against different functional requirements, but a set of cross-cutting criteria applies to all of them. Defining these once avoids drift between ADRs and forces each decision to be honest about the same hard constraints.

## Budget constraint

**Budget is effectively 0€.** This is a first-class filter, not a soft preference. It means:
- Managed cloud services (Confluent Cloud, Datadog, Temporal Cloud, AWS MSK, etc.) are disqualified unless they have a genuinely usable free tier with no credit-card-required production cliff.
- Self-hosted open-source is the default mode.
- Tools with open-core models are acceptable only if the features required by the architecture sit in the free/community tier — the ADR must explicitly verify this.
- Licensing traps (BSL, SSPLv1, ELv2, Commons Clause) must be flagged even if currently free, because they constrain future use.

## Criteria to define

1. **Cost / licensing** — total cost of self-hosting (infra, ops time) vs free tier limits; licence type and change risk.
2. **Regulatory fit** — GDPR (data residency, right to erasure), DORA (resilience testing, RTO/RPO documentation), PSD2 (audit trail, SCA). Hard pass/fail before functional comparison.
3. **Operational complexity at small scale** — how much ops burden does this add to a small team? Preference for tools that degrade gracefully when not actively tuned.
4. **Ecosystem coherence** — does it compose with the rest of the chosen stack without bespoke glue? Native OpenTelemetry, standard connectors, etc.
5. **Exit cost** — how painful is migration away in 3–5 years? Does the tool own a data format or protocol that creates lock-in?
6. **Community and longevity** — is this tool likely to still be maintained in 10 years? Red flags: single-vendor control with recent licence change, stagnant commits, small contributor base.
7. **Functional fit** — tool-specific criteria defined per ADR.

## Deliverable

A markdown section titled '## Common Evaluation Criteria' usable as a template block in each ADR, plus a summary rubric table (criteria × weight) that each ADR fills in for its candidates.
acceptance_criteria: Template section written and agreed. Each ADR-001–010 issue updated to reference this template.

title: ADR series: tool selection for integration implementation

title: Doc 10 update: agent → MCP server trust boundary and customer-identity binding lifecycle
description: Doc 11 (chat agent channel strategy, archie-407) establishes the bank-as-MCP-server pattern with an untrusted third-party LLM agent as the caller. Doc 10's eight-boundary trust model does not currently include this boundary, and the customer-identity binding lifecycle for OAuth-mediated agent sessions (enrolment, SCA, refresh, revocation, recovery from compromised agent credentials) is only briefly mentioned in doc 11. This update should add a ninth trust boundary (Agent → MCP Server) to doc 10's catalogue with its specific failure modes (prompt injection via bank-returned content, hallucinated parameters, confused deputy, token replay across MCP servers, scope creep), and a dedicated section on how an authenticated OAuth session binds to a banking customer (sub claim → client_id), how PSD2 SCA integrates with the initial OAuth grant, how step-up authentication is requested mid-session, refresh/revocation semantics, and what happens when a customer revokes agent access while resource handles are cached.

New top-level 'Customer-Identity Binding Lifecycle (MCP Channel)' section covers enrolment, PSD2 SCA, step-up, refresh/rotation, revocation, cached handles, and compromised credentials. Doc 11 cross-references updated to point to the now-completed treatment.

title: Conceptual doc: chat agent channel strategy — inbound and outbound
description: The system's UI strategy is shifting away from traditional web/mobile frontends toward chat agents (WhatsApp, Slack, or custom LLM-powered agents). This changes the architecture in two directions: (1) Outbound — saga completion and status updates must be delivered as chat messages (via WhatsApp Business API, Slack webhooks, or similar), not SSE streams. This is the async notification problem (tracked separately), but the chat-platform specifics (message formatting, conversation thread continuity, handling multi-step approvals via chat reply) need their own treatment. (2) Inbound — messages arriving from chat platforms are HTTP POST webhooks sent to the bank's edge by the platform (WhatsApp cloud API, Slack Events API). The gateway must route these inbound webhooks to a chat adapter service that interprets natural-language or structured messages as banking commands (constitute deposit, check balance, confirm approval). The chat adapter is itself a bounded context and likely needs an ACL to translate platform-native message formats into domain commands. Decisions needed: which chat platform(s) to support; whether a single adapter handles all platforms or each platform has its own adapter; how conversational context (multi-turn saga flows) is maintained across platform messages; how human approval steps in the saga surface as interactive chat messages (approval buttons, reply-based confirmation). Deliverable: a new conceptual document in integration_concepts/ covering the chat agent channel pattern, its integration points with the existing saga/event backbone, and the trust model for inbound platform webhooks.
notes: Resolved as the bank-as-MCP-server pattern (third-party LLM agent, untrusted caller), not the platform-webhook pattern the original description framed (WhatsApp/Slack). WhatsApp/Slack acknowledged in doc 11 only as user-side surfaces in front of the agent, not as the bank's integration concern. The async-completion subsection describes three patterns (MCP tasks capability per SEP-1686, explicit polling tool, out-of-band callback) and defers callback wire format to archie-087. Two follow-ups filed: archie-0cy (doc 10 trust boundary + customer-identity binding update) and archie-dq6 (ADR-010 MCP runtime selection).
close_reason: Doc 11 (integration_concepts/11-chat-agent-channel-strategy.md) shipped with bank-as-MCP-server framing. The dependency on archie-087 (async callback ADR) is intentionally deferred per the scope decision recorded in notes — doc 11 describes the callback pattern's shape and leaves the wire format to that ADR. README map updated. Follow-ups archie-0cy (doc 10 update) and archie-dq6 (ADR-010 candidate) filed and linked.

title: ADR-011: Async saga completion notification — out-of-band callback wire format
description: The SSE stream_url pattern in ADR-006 and doc 05 assumes an actively waiting client (browser, mobile app). For sagas with workflow-approval steps that take hours or days, SSE is structurally wrong: the connection dies when the client moves on. Chat agents and async clients need a callback/webhook model instead: the initiating request includes a callback_url, and the orchestrator (or a dedicated notification service) posts the terminal outcome to that URL when the saga completes. Decisions needed: (1) callback URL registration — field on the request body vs. a separate subscription endpoint; (2) delivery guarantees — at-least-once with idempotency key on the callback payload; (3) HMAC signature on outbound webhooks so the receiver can verify authenticity; (4) retry policy for failed deliveries (transient network errors, recipient downtime); (5) which component owns delivery — orchestrator directly, or a dedicated notification service that subscribes to saga terminal events from the backbone; (6) whether the existing SSE path and the webhook path coexist (bifurcated by presence of callback_url in the request) or whether SSE is deprecated in favour of webhooks for all clients. Deliverable: decision captured in either a new ADR or as an amendment to ADR-006 and doc 00/05.
close_reason: ADR-011 written: pre-registered subscription endpoint (SSRF mitigation), at-least-once with HMAC-SHA256 + timestamp, exponential backoff 10 attempts over 12h, dedicated notification service as choreography consumer, SSE and callbacks coexist. Four implementation principles: subscription lifecycle, delivery envelope, notification service as choreography consumer, 202 response amendment.

title: Editorial pass on ADR-005 (CQRS read model storage)
description: Three edits: (1) Line 52 MongoDB exclusion claim 'No substitute document store offers sufficient community and ecosystem support to merit evaluation' is too strong — CouchDB (Apache 2.0) and ArangoDB community edition exist. Replace with a narrower claim: 'No substitute open-source document store materially out-performs PostgreSQL for the projection patterns at this scale.' (2) Consider adding a fourth upgrade trigger to the Decision section: what would cause a wholesale revisit rather than per-projection introduction of a specialised paradigm — e.g., 'if measured read SLA exceeds budget across three or more projections simultaneously, re-evaluate the single-storage assumption.' (3) Line 196 materialised view refresh-overlap risk — name the failure mode plainly ('two overlapping refreshes contend for the materialised view's lock; both stall') rather than the abstract 'creates overlap'.
close_reason: Three edits to ADR-005: (1) MongoDB exclusion claim narrowed — names CouchDB and ArangoDB CE as existing open-source substitutes, then argues the narrower point that none materially out-performs PostgreSQL for the projection patterns at this scale, and explicitly reopens the decision if a future projection needs nested-document indexing PostgreSQL jsonb cannot serve; (2) Added a fourth upgrade trigger to the Decision section — three or more simultaneous projection SLA breaches triggers a wholesale paradigm re-evaluation rather than piecemeal addition; (3) Materialised view refresh-blocking risk on line 196 now names the failure mode plainly (overlap contends for the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock at swap, both stall, projection falls progressively behind) instead of the abstract 'creates overlap'.

Conversation topics: PostgreSQL projections vs Elasticsearch vs Redis vs dedicated read DBs per bounded context; write throughput from event replay; query flexibility vs operational simplicity; how the ACL (doc 02) feeds Core Banking data into these projections; cache invalidation and eventual consistency UX implications. Conversation topics: Avro vs Protobuf vs JSON Schema — compatibility rules, tooling, language support; Confluent Schema Registry vs AWS Glue Schema Registry vs Apicurio; forward/backward/full compatibility strategies tied to doc 09 evolution patterns; impact on the event catalog (doc 08). title: ADR-001: Event backbone — message broker choice
description: Decide which message broker to use as the event backbone. The integration_concepts series assumes Kafka in a greenfield context (doc 00, 04), but the decision must be explicit and justified. Conversation topics: Kafka vs Pulsar vs RabbitMQ (streams mode) vs NATS JetStream; durability guarantees; topic compaction and retention for event sourcing; operational complexity in a Portuguese banking context; managed vs self-hosted. Deliverable: ADR-001.md in integration_concepts/adrs/.

title: ADR-010 candidate: MCP server runtime and SDK selection
description: Doc 11 (chat agent channel strategy, archie-407) commits to exposing a bank-owned MCP server as the integration surface for LLM agents but does not pick the runtime, SDK, or transport implementation. Candidates include the official Python SDK (modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk), TypeScript SDK (modelcontextprotocol/typescript-sdk), or a Go/Rust implementation; transport choice between Streamable HTTP (current default for remote servers in MCP spec 2025-11-25) and SSE; hosting model (alongside the existing edge gateway behind Kong from ADR-006, or as a separate service with its own ingress); and the OAuth 2.1 authorisation server integration (existing IAM that already issues JWTs for the REST edge, vs. a dedicated MCP-specific authorisation server with dynamic client registration enabled). This ADR should follow the ADR-000 evaluation framework and reference doc 11 as the conceptual grounding for what the MCP server must support (tools, resources, prompts, elicitation form+url modes, tasks capability per SEP-1686, server-initiated notifications).
close_reason: ADR-010 written: Python SDK + Streamable HTTP + behind Kong + reuse existing IAM with RFC 8707/9728 extensions. Updated doc 11 'How This Connects' table to cross-link ADR-010.

title: Cross-cutting editorial sweep across ADR series
description: Apply consistent edits across all ADRs as a single pass: (1) Audit and strike 'trivially/trivial' usages — if it is trivial, the word is unnecessary; if it is not, the word is wrong. (2) Replace softener phrases ('effectively zero', 'effectively open') with the actual constraint. (3) Audit 'may/should' inside Implementation Principles sections (ADR-003 through ADR-008); principles are normative, so prefer 'must' or declarative present tense. (4) Reduce em-dash density in opening paragraphs and dense analytical passages — three em-dashes per paragraph reads as nested asides. (5) Anchor all relative date phrases ('since 2020', 'as of 2026') to the ADR header date or a specific calendar date.
close_reason: Four targeted edits across the series: (1) ADR-004 line 134 'trivially implemented' -> 'a handful of lines' (the one remaining claim-of-trivial in the series — others matching the grep are legitimate uses of 'non-trivial' meaning 'difficult'); (2) ADR-001 line 75 'effectively zero' -> 'negligible' (the assertive form); (3) ADR-002 line 89 'effectively seamless' -> 'seamless'; (4) ADR-007 P4 'should use pseudonymous identifiers wherever possible' rewritten to 'must default to pseudonymous identifiers; raw identifiers require an explicit justification at the call site that survives code review' — strengthens the normative verb while preserving the legitimate exception path. Deliberately did NOT do: em-dash reduction (28-44 per file is mostly structural use, not nested asides — flattening it would damage the author's voice for negligible clarity gain) and broad date-anchor sweep (almost all 'as of YEAR' / 'in YEAR' references already carry a year, which is itself an anchor; the residual unanchored 'since 2020' was already fixed in P2). Most 'may/should' inside Implementation Principles are normatively-correct prohibitions ('No saga may hold...') or permissions ('Services may add...').
